title: The narrow gate (Matthew 7:13–14)
hook: the way to life is narrow, and few find it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden rule: do for others what you'd hope they'd do for you. Your line was as you would be treated.

A stadium is letting out. Thousands of people, all pouring toward the big main gates, the wide ramps, the parking lots. It's easy. You don't even have to decide; the crowd carries you. Off to one side, there's a small door in a wall. You'd have to step out of the flow to find it. You might have to turn sideways to get through. Nobody's holding it open. Jesus, near the end of his sermon, draws exactly that picture: two gates, two roads, and a crowd.
screen: `THE STADIUM LETS OUT.` → `THE CROWD CARRIES YOU.` → `A SMALL DOOR IN A WALL.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat." Notice the spelling: strait, s-t-r-a-i-t. Not straight, like a ruler. Strait means narrow, tight, like the Strait of Gibraltar, a narrow stretch of sea. Some say the phrase the straight and narrow grew out of this verse, with strait heard as straight. The Greek word is stenē: narrow, cramped. Then verse fourteen: "Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it." The word narrow there is even more vivid: pressed, squeezed, the way a crowd presses on you. It shares a root with the Greek word for trouble or hardship. So the road to life isn't described as pleasant. It's a squeeze. What makes it narrow? The sermon itself: love your enemies, give in secret, don't judge, don't worry, do to others what you'd want. None of that is complicated. All of it is hard. Christians read the few who find it in more than one way. Some hear a sober warning about salvation. Others hear a description of discipleship: the way of the sermon is uncommon, and the crowd often goes the other direction. Both readings agree on this: you don't drift through a narrow gate. You have to choose it, one step out of the flow.
screen: `STRAIT, NOT STRAIGHT.` · `STENĒ: NARROW, CRAMPED.` · `A WAY THAT PRESSES.` · `YOU HAVE TO CHOOSE IT.`

segments.voice: Think of one choice waiting for you today, with an easy way and a harder right way: the apology you've been putting off, the honest answer instead of the smooth one, the call you keep not making. Don't solve it yet. Just picture the two gates, the wide one you'd slide through without thinking and the narrow one, and see yourself stepping sideways toward it.
Stene, the Greek word for narrow, cramped, pressed on every side. The gate is strait, meaning tight, and the way to life is a squeeze you have to choose.
Your line: the narrow way. It's tight, and it leads to life. Two hundred fifty-eight days in.

howItsDone: Some Christians hear this passage as a call to deliberate, daily choices that go against the easy way, and some churches use it in preaching about discipleship and conversion.

chat.says: Is 'strait gate' just an old spelling of 'straight gate'?
options: No, strait means narrow and tight; the way to life is a squeeze you choose.
Yes, it means a gate lined up perfectly straight with the road.
Yes, it means a path with no bends, easy to walk without trying.
